subject: Nobody notices clean — until the day it slips
preheader: A written scope, audits on a schedule, one team accountable by name.
hero_alt: Uniformed janitorial crew mid-shift in a bright lobby
headline: Nobody notices clean. Everybody notices the day it slips.
body_paragraph_1: Cleaning is the only service in your building judged every single day and reported only when it fails. By the time a tenant emails about the restroom, the program has drifted for weeks.
body_paragraph_2: Ours is built so the standard is written down, someone owns it by name, and it gets checked before you have to. Daily, periodic and deep-clean tasks are defined by area and frequency.
point_1_body: Daily, periodic and deep-clean tasks written by area and frequency — so "clean" means the same thing to both teams.
point_2_body: Quality auditors inspect proactively and log what they find. You see the report whether or not anything was wrong.
point_3_body: Our teams work in Corrigo, ServiceChannel, FacilitySource and FEXA, so requests close where you already track them.
aside_body: Cleaning is a people business, and turnover is what breaks it. We hire selectively — only 5% of applicants are brought on — train through master trainers, and give every site a named account executive.

subject: Your cleaning program is one no-show from a complaint
preheader: See the audit report whether or not anything went wrong.
hero_alt: Close-up: gloved hand wiping a spotless restroom fixture
headline: Clean isn't a mop. It's a management system.
body_paragraph_1: A cleaning program rarely fails all at once. It slips — a missed detail here, a skipped task there — until the complaints start and you're managing a problem instead of a schedule.
body_paragraph_2: We fix drift with structure: a documented scope, proactive audits you can see, and requests that close inside the systems you already use.
point_1_body: Every task, area and frequency is documented, so the standard doesn't live in someone's head.
point_2_body: We catch drift before you do, and show you the check either way.
point_3_body: No new portal to learn — we close the work in the system you already use.
aside_body: The program is only as good as the people on it. We're selective on hiring, serious on training, and we put a name on every account.

subject: The restroom is your reputation, checked daily
preheader: Only 5% of applicants make our team. Here's why that matters.
hero_alt: Team lead reviewing a cleaning checklist on a tablet
headline: The standard is written down — and someone owns it by name.
body_paragraph_1: The difference between a clean building and a complaint isn't effort. It's whether the standard is written down and whether someone is accountable for it by name.
body_paragraph_2: We hire selectively, train through master trainers, and give every site a named account executive — so the people in your building are why it stays clean.
point_1_body: You approve the scope up front; we deliver to it, not to interpretation.
point_2_body: Inspections are scheduled, not triggered by a complaint.
point_3_body: Requests start and finish where your team already looks.
aside_body: Consistency comes from people, not promises: selective hiring, real training, and a named contact who owns your site.

subject: The work order you forgot is the one that floods
preheader: One scope, one invoice, one number for every trade.
hero_alt: Technician fixing an HVAC/plumbing unit in a mechanical room
headline: The small repair you defer is the one that floods the floor below.
body_paragraph_1: The repair you meant to get to is the one that turns into water on the floor below. Deferred work orders don't disappear — they compound, and on their timeline, not yours.
body_paragraph_2: We put every trade on one scope, one invoice and one number, and close the work inside the system you already track. Our own teams and vetted partners handle the rest.
point_1_body: Every trade routes through one scope and one system, so nothing gets handled off-book or forgotten.
point_2_body: Work is tracked to completion in your system, so you see status without chasing anyone.
point_3_body: One scope, one invoice, one number — instead of reconciling five vendors every month.
aside_body: The trades we send are vetted, insured and accountable — not whoever was available. One standard applies whether it's our crew or a partner.

subject: Small repairs get expensive when they wait
preheader: Deferred work orders don't disappear — they compound.
hero_alt: Maintenance tech with tool bag walking a corridor
headline: One work-order system for every trade in the building.
body_paragraph_1: Most buildings run repairs through a patchwork of vendors, each with its own number, invoice and excuse. The gaps between them are where things break twice.
body_paragraph_2: Painting, restoration, lighting, HVAC, plumbing and more — dispatched, tracked and closed in one place, so nothing falls through the gap between vendors.
point_1_body: Painting, lighting, HVAC, plumbing and more — one documented program instead of a stack of vendors.
point_2_body: Nothing sits 'pending' quietly — the loop closes where you already track it.
point_3_body: The whole building's work lands on a single, predictable invoice.
aside_body: Behind one number is a bench of vetted trade partners, coordinated so the work closes cleanly.

subject: One number for every repair in the building
preheader: Vetted trade partners, dispatched and closed in your system.
hero_alt: Two techs coordinating a repair on a work-order tablet
headline: Repairs shouldn't need three vendors and four phone calls.
body_paragraph_1: When a fix needs three calls and four days, small problems become expensive ones. A single accountable team closes the loop before that happens.
body_paragraph_2: You get a named account executive and client service manager, not a queue — so the person who answers knows your building.
point_1_body: The scope is written and priced against what the building actually needs, not a template.
point_2_body: You get visibility from request to done, on every trade.
point_3_body: No vendor maze: one point of contact for everything.
aside_body: We stand behind every trade on the contract, our own and our partners' alike.

subject: Your lobby is the first thing anyone judges
preheader: Trained, uniformed coverage — not a rotating cast of temps.
hero_alt: Sharp, uniformed concierge at a modern lobby desk
headline: Your lobby introduces the building before anyone says a word.
body_paragraph_1: Your lobby introduces the building before anyone says a word. A staffed, sharp front-of-house says the property is well run; a gap at the desk says the opposite — loudly.
body_paragraph_2: We staff front-of-house with trained, uniformed people and back them with a named account executive — so coverage is consistent and the standard is owned.
point_1_body: Front-of-house is staffed by trained, uniformed people to a written standard — not whoever the agency sent.
point_2_body: Every site gets a named account executive and client service manager — a person, not a ticket queue.
point_3_body: Security and concierge sit on the same contract as cleaning and maintenance — one relationship, not another RFP.
aside_body: Coverage means little if the person is wrong for your lobby. We hire selectively and train to your building's standard, so the desk reflects the property.

subject: Coverage gaps are what tenants remember

hero_alt: Security officer greeting a visitor at the entrance
headline: Coverage gaps are what tenants remember.
body_paragraph_1: Front-of-house is judged constantly and remembered at its worst. One uncovered shift or one indifferent greeting is what a tenant carries into a renewal conversation.
body_paragraph_2: Security and concierge run on the same contract as the rest of your program, with one point of accountability instead of another vendor to manage.
point_1_body: Coverage is defined shift by shift, so there are no quiet gaps at the desk.
point_2_body: You call someone who knows your building, not whoever picks up.
point_3_body: Same team, same standard, same accountability across every service.
aside_body: Front-of-house is a hiring problem first. We're selective, we train, and we keep the same faces in place.

subject: A front desk that reflects the building, not a temp agency

point_2_body: Accountability has a name and a number.
point_3_body: No separate staffing vendor to manage on the side.
aside_body: The person at your desk is chosen and trained for it — not a rotating cast of temps.

subject: The pest problem tenants report before you see it
preheader: P1 Pest Solutions — our pest division, same contract.
hero_alt: P1 technician placing a monitor in a back-of-house area
headline: Tenants report pests before property managers ever see them.
body_paragraph_1: Pests are the one problem tenants usually spot before you do. By the time it reaches your inbox, it's a reputation issue, not just a maintenance one.
body_paragraph_2: P1 Pest Solutions is our pest division — commercial-grade treatment on the same contract, invoice and point of contact as everything else we do.
point_1_body: We target the harborage — cracks, voids, equipment cavities — not just the surfaces you can see.
point_2_body: Monitors between visits tell us whether the population is falling — so you get a trend, not a guess.
point_3_body: Pest control runs on the same contract, invoice and contact as the rest of your program.
aside_body: Commercial pest work lives or dies on the record. We document what we find and do, so you're covered for audits, brand standards and corporate.

subject: Pest control belongs on the same contract
preheader: Commercial pest control built for audits and records.
hero_alt: Tech inspecting under equipment with a flashlight
headline: Pest control belongs on the same contract as everything else.
body_paragraph_1: Most buildings bolt pest control on as a separate vendor with a separate invoice and separate promises. It doesn't have to live outside the rest of your program.
body_paragraph_2: We treat the harborage, not the surface, and leave a written record of what was found and done — built for audits, not just for show.
point_1_body: Treatment goes where pests actually live and travel, with monitors between visits.
point_2_body: We measure results between services, not just show up and spray.
point_3_body: P1 is our division, not a subcontractor — coordinated with everything else on-site.
aside_body: P1 is built for commercial reality: targeted treatment, monitoring, and a written trail your auditor will accept.

subject: One vendor for the whole building — pests included
preheader: One vendor, one invoice, pests included.
hero_alt: Clean commercial kitchen with monitor stations in place
headline: One building, one program — pests included.
body_paragraph_1: Commercial pest work is about the record as much as the result — what was found, what was treated, and proof for your audit file.
body_paragraph_2: One vendor for the whole building means pest work is coordinated with cleaning and maintenance, not fighting them.
point_1_body: Every placement and finding is documented for your file.
point_2_body: You see whether it's working, backed by the record.
point_3_body: One relationship covers the building, pests included.
aside_body: The result matters; the proof matters as much. Every visit leaves a documented record.

subject: Winter grime is hard on floors and first impressions
preheader: Floor care, deep cleans and daily standards, all written down.
hero_alt: Crew running a floor scrubber across a wet-look lobby floor
headline: Winter drags grime through your front door every day.
body_paragraph_1: Winter walks straight through your front door. Salt, slush and grit ride in on every shoe and land on the floors visitors judge first.
body_paragraph_2: We handle the season's grime on a schedule — entrance mats, daily attention to high-traffic floors, and periodic deep cleans that keep finish intact.
point_1_body: Floor care, restrooms and deep cleans are written by area and frequency, so winter grime doesn't win.
point_2_body: Quality auditors inspect proactively and log what they find. You see the report whether or not anything was wrong.
point_3_body: Our teams work in Corrigo, ServiceChannel, FacilitySource and FEXA, so requests close where you already track them.
aside_body: Winter is when programs slip and people quit. We hire selectively, train through master trainers, and keep a named contact on your account through the season.

subject: Salt, slush and traffic — your floors take the season hardest
preheader: We handle the grime the season drags in.
hero_alt: Entrance mats and squeegee work by the doors in winter
headline: Salt and slush are hard on floors and first impressions.
body_paragraph_1: The season is hardest on the surfaces that matter most — entrances, lobbies and the floors that set a first impression the moment someone walks in.
body_paragraph_2: Floor care, restroom standards and deep cleans are written into the scope by area and frequency, so winter doesn't quietly erode the building.
point_1_body: The high-traffic surfaces get defined daily attention, not occasional catch-up.
point_2_body: We catch winter drift before you do, and show you the check either way.
point_3_body: No new portal — floor-care requests close in the system you already use.
aside_body: The season tests consistency, and consistency is a people problem. We staff and train so the standard holds.

subject: The lobby floor tells visitors how the building is run
preheader: The details visitors notice, managed on a schedule.
hero_alt: Polished floor reflecting overhead lights, crew behind
headline: The lobby floor tells visitors how the building is run.
body_paragraph_1: Floor care isn't cosmetic in winter. Grit left on hard floors grinds finish down and turns a maintained surface into a replacement line item.
body_paragraph_2: Our crews are trained and accountable by name, so the details visitors notice are managed, not left to chance.
point_1_body: You approve the schedule; we hold it through the season.
point_2_body: Inspections are scheduled, not triggered by a complaint.
point_3_body: Work starts and finishes where your team already looks.
aside_body: The details that survive winter are the ones a trained, accountable crew is responsible for by name.

subject: The cheapest repair is the one you schedule
preheader: Inspections, filters, coils and repairs before the cold finds them.
hero_alt: Tech changing rooftop HVAC filters in cold weather
headline: The cheapest repair is the one you scheduled in advance.
body_paragraph_1: The first cold snap doesn't create problems so much as reveal the ones you deferred all year. Heating systems fail on the coldest night, not a convenient one.
body_paragraph_2: We handle the inspection, the filters, the coils and the repairs — so the first cold night is uneventful instead of an emergency.
points_label: HOW WE STAY AHEAD OF IT
point_1_body: Heating, cooling and building systems are inspected on a schedule, not when they fail.
point_2_body: Anything found on a preventive visit is logged and closed as a work order in your system.
point_3_body: One number for every system, with vetted trade partners for the specialty work.
aside_body: Preventive work depends on the team behind it. Our own crews plus vetted, insured trade partners keep every system on schedule.

subject: Cold snaps find every system you deferred
preheader: Preventive maintenance that keeps small problems small.
hero_alt: Maintenance inspecting a boiler room with a checklist
headline: Cold snaps find every system you deferred.
body_paragraph_1: Preventive maintenance is the cheapest work you'll do all winter, because the alternative is an emergency call at the worst time and price.
body_paragraph_2: Preventive visits are scheduled and documented, and anything we find closes as a work order in the system you already use.
point_1_body: Preventive tasks are documented by system and interval, so nothing is assumed.
point_2_body: Findings don't get lost between visits — they're documented and tracked to done.
point_3_body: You call one place; we coordinate the trades behind it.
aside_body: One accountable team, one bench of vetted partners — so nothing waits on 'who do we call.'

subject: Preventive maintenance before winter does the finding
preheader: One call for every system in the building.
hero_alt: Frost on a window, warm interior, tech at work

body_paragraph_1: Every system in the building has a season. Heading into winter, the ones you haven't inspected are the ones most likely to find you first.
body_paragraph_2: One team, one number, and vetted trade partners for the specialty work — so every system is covered before the season tests it.
point_1_body: We check the things that fail in winter before winter arrives.
point_2_body: You see what we checked and what we fixed, on the record.
point_3_body: Every system covered under one accountable contract.
aside_body: We keep the specialty trades vetted and ready, so preventive work actually happens on time.

subject: Your heating fails on the coldest night, not a convenient one
preheader: Inspection, filters, coils and repairs before the season loads the system.
hero_alt: Tech servicing a rooftop heating unit, cold sky
headline: Your heating system will fail on the coldest night — not a convenient one.
body_paragraph_1: Your heating equipment has been idle for months and is about to run flat-out. Dirt, wear and deferred fixes are the leading causes of a system failing exactly when you need it most.
body_paragraph_2: We handle the inspection, the filters, the coils and the repairs, so the first cold night is uneventful. One contract covers heating now and cooling in spring.
tip_headline: A Clean System Is a Cheaper System
tip_body: Replacing a dirty filter with a clean one can cut a unit's energy use by 5 to 15 percent. Pair it with a coil and lighting check and the savings land on the same bill.
note_body: Service cooling equipment in spring and heating in fall — contractors book solid the week the weather turns.

subject: The first cold snap finds every system you deferred
preheader: Contractors book solid the week the weather turns.
hero_alt: Boiler-room inspection with a checklist
headline: The first cold snap doesn't cause problems. It reveals the ones you deferred.
body_paragraph_1: The first real cold doesn't create problems so much as reveal the ones that sat all year — and it reveals them on the coldest night, at emergency rates.
body_paragraph_2: We inspect proactively, document what we find, and close any repair in the system you already use — before the weather forces the issue.
tip_headline: Filters Are the Cheapest Repair You'll Make
tip_body: A clogged filter forces the system to work harder to move the same air, driving up energy use and shortening equipment life. Monthly checks pay for themselves.
note_body: The first cold week is when every building calls at once; scheduling now means you're not in that line.

subject: Book heating service before the week the weather turns
preheader: We handle heating and cooling on one contract.
hero_alt: Thermostat handoff in a warm, lit lobby
headline: The cheapest heating repair is the one you schedule in September.
body_paragraph_1: Heating service is cheap and boring in September. In January it's an emergency call, if you can get one — contractors book solid the week the weather turns.
body_paragraph_2: Our own teams and vetted trade partners keep every system on schedule, so you're not competing for a contractor when everyone else needs one too.
tip_headline: Heat Rises — So Do Deferred Repairs
tip_body: Deferred heating repairs don't get cheaper with time — they get more expensive and more urgent. The fix scheduled now is the emergency you avoid in January.
note_body: Heating tune-ups booked before October are routine; booked in January they're emergencies.

subject: The gaps you can't see are the ones winter finds
preheader: Seals, gutters and exterior gaps, handled before the cold gets in.
hero_alt: Worker sealing exterior window/door gaps
headline: The gaps you can't see are the ones winter finds first.
body_paragraph_1: Warm air leaves and cold air gets in through gaps you never see — around doors, windows, docks and roof penetrations. Every one is a line on your winter energy bill.
body_paragraph_2: We walk the envelope, seal what's leaking, and handle gutters, drainage and exterior gaps on one scope — before the first freeze locks it all in.
tip_headline: A Dollar of Sealant Saves Ten in Heat
tip_body: Sealing air leaks around doors, windows and penetrations is one of the highest-return maintenance dollars you can spend before winter.
note_body: Weatherization done before the first freeze locks in savings for the whole season.

subject: Seal it now or heat the parking lot all winter
preheader: Small drafts are big energy bills by January.
hero_alt: Gutter cleaning from a ladder, fall leaves
headline: Every draft is a line on January's energy bill.
body_paragraph_1: Weatherization is the least glamorous work you'll do all year and among the highest-return. A weekend of sealing offsets months of overworked heating.
body_paragraph_2: It's one walkthrough now against an emergency and a utility spike later. We mark what needs sealing and price it against what the building needs.
tip_body: A gap you can't feel in October is a draft you can't ignore in January. Small leaks add up to a real share of heating cost.
note_body: Exterior sealing gets harder and costlier once temperatures drop — October is the window.

subject: Weatherize in October, skip the January emergency
preheader: One walkthrough now saves an emergency later.
hero_alt: Weatherstripping a loading-dock door
headline: Seal it in October, or heat the outdoors until March.
body_paragraph_1: The building envelope is your first defense against winter. Handled in October it's routine; discovered in January it's an emergency and a utility bill.
body_paragraph_2: Weatherization runs on the same contract as everything else, so there's one number to call and one team accountable for the result.
tip_body: The building envelope quietly determines your winter energy bill. Tightening it once pays back every cold month that follows.
note_body: Gutters and drainage cleared before the leaves finish falling save you a mid-winter emergency.

subject: One slip on your walkway is a claim, not an inconvenience
preheader: Salt, plows and crews on standby before the first flake.
hero_alt: Crew salting/plowing a commercial walkway at dawn
headline: One slip on an uncleared walk is a claim, not an inconvenience.
body_paragraph_1: Snow and ice turn every walkway, entrance and lot into a liability the moment they land. One slip on an uncleared surface is a claim, not an inconvenience.
body_paragraph_2: We stage salt, equipment and crews before the season and respond on a defined trigger, so your walks and lots are clear before the first foot hits them.
tip_headline: Ice Doesn't Forgive a Slow Start
tip_body: Pre-treating walks and lots before a storm keeps ice from bonding, which makes clearing faster and surfaces safer. Prevention costs a fraction of a claim.
note_body: Snow contracts signed before the season guarantee you a crew when the storm actually hits.

subject: Snow doesn't wait for a purchase order
preheader: Slip-and-fall claims start on an uncleared walk.
hero_alt: Snowplow clearing a parking lot
headline: Snow doesn't wait for a purchase order.
body_paragraph_1: Winter weather doesn't schedule around your purchase orders. The storm arrives, and either your crew is already assigned or you're calling around at 5 a.m.
body_paragraph_2: Snow, ice and slip-and-fall prevention run on the same contract as the rest of your program — one scope, one invoice, one number when it storms.
tip_headline: The Cheapest Claim Is One You Prevent
tip_body: Most slip-and-fall incidents happen on surfaces that were 'about to be' cleared. A defined response trigger removes the guesswork.
note_body: The buildings that stay clear are the ones that arranged coverage before the first flake.

subject: Lock in snow-and-ice coverage before the first storm
preheader: One number for snow, ice and everything else.
hero_alt: Wet-floor caution and mats at a snowy entrance
headline: The first storm is a bad time to start looking for a plow.
body_paragraph_1: Slip-and-fall exposure rides along with every storm. The buildings that stay clear are the ones that arranged coverage before the season started.
body_paragraph_2: We handle the clearing, the treatment and the documentation, so coverage is arranged long before the forecast turns.
tip_body: Documented clearing times aren't just safety — they're your defense if a claim ever lands.
note_body: Salt and equipment get scarce mid-storm; pre-season staging avoids the shortage.

subject: The building doesn't close for the holidays — neither do we
preheader: Live dispatch every day of the year, no answering service.
hero_alt: Dispatcher on a headset at night, phones live
headline: The building doesn't close for the holidays. Neither does the phone.
body_paragraph_1: The building doesn't close for the holidays, and neither do the things that break. A boiler, a leak or a security gap on December 26 doesn't care that the office is dark.
body_paragraph_2: We answer with a live dispatcher 24/7/365 — no answering service — and back it with our own teams and vetted partners for whatever the call turns out to be.
tip_headline: A Live Voice Beats a Voicemail
tip_body: After-hours problems get worse waiting for a callback. A live dispatcher turns a two-day emergency into a same-night fix.
note_body: Confirm holiday coverage now — the week between holidays is the hardest to staff after the fact.

subject: Who answers when something breaks on December 26?
preheader: Holiday coverage that doesn't skip a beat.
hero_alt: Lit building exterior, holiday quiet
headline: Something will break on December 26. Who answers?
body_paragraph_1: Year-end is exactly when coverage thins out and problems don't. The question isn't whether something happens over the holidays — it's who picks up when it does.
body_paragraph_2: One contract covers repairs, security and facilities straight through the holidays, so a problem on the 26th is our problem, not yours.
tip_body: The holidays are when small issues become big ones simply because no one's watching. Continuous coverage closes that gap.
note_body: Year-end is when most vendors go quiet; a 24/7 contract means yours doesn't.

subject: 24/7/365 live dispatch, no answering service
preheader: One call for repairs, security and facilities — even on the 25th.
hero_alt: Tech responding to an after-hours call, keys in hand
headline: 24/7/365 live dispatch — a real person, not an answering service.
body_paragraph_1: Most vendors route you to an answering service after hours. Ours routes you to a live dispatcher, every day of the year, because that's when buildings actually need help.
body_paragraph_2: Coverage doesn't thin out because the calendar says holiday. The same accountable team is on, documented and reachable, every day of the year.
tip_headline: Coverage Is Cheapest Before You Need It
tip_body: Confirm before the break who answers your building's emergency line — and whether it's a person or a machine.
note_body: Line up emergency coverage before the break, not during it.

subject: A frozen pipe is a five-figure problem that starts at 32°
preheader: We know which pipes freeze first and check them before they do.
hero_alt: Insulated pipes in a cold mechanical room
headline: A frozen pipe is a five-figure problem that starts at 32 degrees.
body_paragraph_1: A frozen pipe is one of the most expensive things that can happen to a building, and it starts quietly at 32 degrees in a spot nobody was watching.
body_paragraph_2: We know which pipes freeze first — the exterior runs, the unheated corners — and check and protect them before the temperature does the testing.
tip_headline: 32 Degrees Is the Warning, Not the Problem
tip_body: Letting a faucet trickle during extreme cold keeps water moving and can prevent a freeze — a cheap habit against an expensive failure.
note_body: The deepest cold usually lands in January; protecting exposed pipes before then is the cheap move.

subject: The deep freeze finds the pipe you forgot about
preheader: Frozen pipes don't wait for business hours.
hero_alt: Tech checking an exposed pipe with a thermal reading
headline: The deep freeze always finds the pipe you forgot about.
body_paragraph_1: Deep cold finds the weak point — the uninsulated run, the exterior wall, the pipe on the wrong side of a door. By the time it bursts, prevention is off the table.
body_paragraph_2: Prevention and emergency response live on one contract: we insulate and monitor the weak points, and we're a live call away if the cold wins anyway.
tip_body: Know your building's first-to-freeze runs — usually exterior walls and unheated spaces — and insulate them before the cold tests them.
note_body: Cold-snap prep is worthless the day the snap arrives — the value is all in doing it early.

subject: Cold-snap coverage before the temperature drops
preheader: Emergency response and prevention on one contract.
hero_alt: Frost on an exterior wall, warm interior beyond
headline: By the time a pipe bursts, prevention is off the table.
body_paragraph_1: The difference between a cold snap and a flooded floor is usually a single unheated pipe. Knowing which one, and checking it early, is the whole game.
body_paragraph_2: We document what we protect and close any fix in your system, so cold-snap readiness is a plan, not a scramble.
tip_body: A pipe that freezes doesn't always burst immediately; catching it early can be the difference between a thaw and a flood.
note_body: Know your at-risk pipes before the forecast, not after the flood.

subject: Ice dams do their damage where you can't see it
preheader: Roof load, ice dams and drainage, checked before the thaw.
hero_alt: Icicles / ice dam along a commercial roof edge
headline: Ice dams do their most expensive work where you can't see it.
body_paragraph_1: Late winter is when the season's damage comes due. Ice dams, roof load and blocked drainage do their work slowly and out of sight, then show up on your ceiling.
body_paragraph_2: We check roof load, clear ice dams and keep drainage moving, so the thaw runs off the building instead of into it.
tip_headline: Snow Has Weight — Respect the Limit
tip_body: Keep roof drains and downspouts clear so meltwater leaves the building instead of pooling and refreezing at the edge.
note_body: Late-winter thaw-and-refreeze is when hidden roof damage surfaces; check before it does.

subject: The snow on your roof has weight — and a limit
preheader: The damage you can't see is the expensive kind.
hero_alt: Roof crew clearing snow load
headline: The snow on your roof has weight — and a limit.
body_paragraph_1: Snow on a roof has real weight, and every roof has a limit. Thaw-and-refreeze is what turns accumulation into an ice dam and an ice dam into a leak.
body_paragraph_2: Roof, gutters and the damage winter hides run on the same contract, with one team accountable and one number to call.
tip_headline: Clear the Dam Before It Leaks
tip_body: Ice dams form when heat escaping the roof melts snow that refreezes at the cold eaves. Ventilation and clearing break the cycle.
note_body: Roof and gutter issues found in February are cheaper than the ceiling repair in March.

subject: Late-winter roof checks before the thaw does the finding
preheader: One team for roofs, gutters and what winter leaves behind.
hero_alt: Ceiling water stain being inspected indoors
headline: Late winter is when deferred roof problems come due.
body_paragraph_1: The problems that started in December don't announce themselves until February — usually as a water stain, always at a bad time.
body_paragraph_2: We inspect proactively and document what we find, so late-winter problems close as work orders instead of surprises on your ceiling.
tip_body: A quick roof-load check after a heavy snow is cheap insurance against a structural surprise.
note_body: Schedule the roof check between storms, not after the leak.

subject: The pallet came in. So did the mice.
preheader: We seal the entry points and treat the harborage — with a record for your file.
hero_alt: P1 tech sealing a gap along a warehouse dock door
headline: MICE DON'T MOVE IN WHEN IT'S COLD. THEY MOVE IN BEFORE.
body_paragraph_1: Rodents don't wait for the first hard freeze to come inside — they move ahead of it, following warmth and food through gaps you'd never think twice about. A quarter-inch opening is all a mouse needs.
body_paragraph_2: We treat the harborage, not the surface. We seal the entry points, place targeted control where rodents actually travel, and set monitors that show whether pressure is dropping between visits — with a written record for your file.
points_label: THREE ENTRY POINTS WE ALWAYS CHECK
point_1_body: Cardboard and pallets are the most common ride in.
point_2_body: Gaps around pipes and conduit let rodents into the walls.
point_3_body: Food, warmth and clutter in one place draw rodents fast.
note_body: Store product on wire racks a few inches off the floor and away from walls. A mouse needs cover to travel; take it away and the whole building turns hostile to them.

subject: A gap the width of a pencil is a front door for a mouse
preheader: Rodents follow warmth and food indoors before the first frost.
hero_alt: Bait-station placement along an interior wall base
headline: ONE GAP THE WIDTH OF A PENCIL IS A FRONT DOOR FOR A MOUSE.
body_paragraph_1: In October, every rodent within range is looking for a warm place with food and quiet. A commercial building offers all three, and one uncontested gap is an open invitation.
body_paragraph_2: Our technicians map the runs, close the gaps and document every placement. You get a program built for an audit, not a can of spray and a handshake.
point_1_body: Gaps under dock doors are a nightly rodent highway.
point_2_body: Unsealed penetrations are the interior route between rooms.
point_3_body: Crumbs and open packaging keep a population fed all winter.
note_body: Walk your dock doors at dusk and look for daylight underneath. Any gap you can see under a door, a rodent can use — and will.

subject: By the time you see one mouse, there isn't one
preheader: Commercial rodent control built for audits, not just traps.
hero_alt: Flashlight inspection behind stored pallets
headline: BY THE TIME YOU SEE ONE, THERE ISN'T ONE.
body_paragraph_1: The reason you rarely see the first mouse is that rodents stay out of sight until the population forces them into the open. By then it's not one mouse — it's a colony with a routine.
body_paragraph_2: One scope, one invoice, one number to call — with monitors and reporting that show the population trend, not just a service date.
point_1_body: Every delivery is a chance for a stowaway.
point_2_body: Wall voids are warm, quiet and out of sight — ideal harborage.
point_3_body: Dry storage with gaps behind shelving is a nesting favorite.
note_body: The first droppings show up along wall bases and behind equipment, not in the open. That's where an inspection should start, and where a monitor earns its keep.

subject: The pests you stopped seeing didn't leave — they moved in
preheader: We find where they're overwintering and close it before spring.
hero_alt: Tech inspecting wall voids / utility penetrations
headline: THEY'RE NOT GONE FOR WINTER. THEY'RE INSIDE YOUR WALLS.
body_paragraph_1: The pests that seem to vanish in November didn't leave. Cluster flies, stink bugs, spiders and rodents overwinter — often inside wall voids, attics and utility chases — waiting out the cold in your building.
body_paragraph_2: We find where they're overwintering — voids, penetrations, attics — and treat and seal it before spring turns dormant into active. Every placement and finding goes on the record.
point_1_body: Cluster flies and stink bugs pack into warm voids for winter.
point_2_body: Gaps in framing are the classic overwintering entry.
point_3_body: Quiet, undisturbed rooms are where spiders and rodents settle.
note_body: Seal exterior cracks and vents in the fall, before overwintering pests move in — once they're settled in the voids, treatment gets harder and slower.

subject: Overwintering pests pick their building in the fall
preheader: Cluster flies, stink bugs and rodents settle in for the season — in your building.
hero_alt: Monitor devices along a back corridor
headline: OVERWINTERING PESTS PICK YOUR BUILDING IN THE FALL.
body_paragraph_1: Overwintering pests choose their shelter in the fall, and a commercial structure with warm voids and quiet corners is prime real estate. The decision they make now determines what emerges in spring.
body_paragraph_2: We go after the shelter, not the symptom, with targeted placements in the cracks and voids where overwintering pests settle, and monitors that track what's happening behind the walls.
point_1_body: Upper voids hold heat and go unchecked for months.
point_2_body: Foundation and siding cracks are fall entry points.
point_3_body: Warmth and clutter make ideal winter harborage.
note_body: A warm week in winter can wake overwintering flies inside the walls; if you see them at windows in January, the harborage is interior, not outdoor.

subject: What's living in your walls until spring?
preheader: Targeted treatment and a written record, harborage first.
hero_alt: Exterior foundation inspection in late fall
headline: THE PESTS YOU STOP SEEING IN NOVEMBER DIDN'T LEAVE.
body_paragraph_1: Winter quiet is deceptive. Behind the walls, overwintering populations are dormant, not gone, and the spring 'sudden appearance' is really months of undisturbed harborage coming to light.
body_paragraph_2: You get a documented program and a single point of contact, so the work is coordinated and provable — built for your audit file, not just for the moment.
point_1_body: Vertical chases move pests between floors unseen.
point_2_body: Unscreened vents invite pests into the structure.
point_3_body: The space above tiles is warm, dark and rarely inspected.
note_body: Note where you find dormant clusters now — those exact spots are where next spring's activity will emerge, and where prevention pays off.

subject: The holiday rush feeds more than your customers
preheader: Sanitation and monitoring that keep the season's food from feeding pests.
hero_alt: Clean commercial kitchen with monitors in place
headline: MORE FOOD, MORE TRAFFIC, MORE FOR PESTS TO FIND.
body_paragraph_1: The holidays push more food, more deliveries and more foot traffic through your building than any other time — and every bit is something for pests to find, especially where sanitation slips under pressure.
body_paragraph_2: We focus on sanitation and monitoring where the season's risk actually is — drains, dry storage, back-of-house — and leave a clean, written record through your busiest, most-scrutinized weeks.
point_1_body: Organic film in drains breeds small flies fast.
point_2_body: Overflowing bins in December are a magnet.
point_3_body: Heat and debris under fixtures shelter roaches.
note_body: A floor drain with organic film is a fly breeding site, not a clean drain. Enzyme cleaning during the holiday rush prevents a January problem.

subject: A slow drain now is a fruit-fly problem in January
preheader: Drains, dry storage and back-of-house — checked and documented.
hero_alt: Tech inspecting floor drains in a food-prep area
headline: THE HOLIDAY RUSH FEEDS MORE THAN YOUR CUSTOMERS.
body_paragraph_1: December is when back-of-house discipline is hardest to hold and easiest for pests to exploit. A slow drain, an overflowing bin or a missed clean-down becomes a breeding site fast.
body_paragraph_2: We treat the conditions, not just the pest: harborage, moisture and food sources get identified and addressed, with monitors that flag a problem before it becomes a complaint.
point_1_body: Spilled product feeds stored-product pests unseen.
point_2_body: Holiday deliveries bring pests in on the goods.
point_3_body: Sugar residue and drips feed ants and flies.
note_body: Break down and remove cartons the day they land; stacked cardboard in a back corridor is harborage, not storage.

subject: More food, more traffic, more for pests to find
preheader: A clean audit trail through your busiest month.
hero_alt: Back-of-house dry-storage inspection
headline: A SLOW DRAIN IN DECEMBER IS A FRUIT-FLY FACTORY IN JANUARY.
body_paragraph_1: Stored-product pests and small flies don't need much — a spill in dry storage, organic film in a floor drain — and the busiest month is exactly when those conditions pile up unnoticed.
body_paragraph_2: One coordinated program keeps pest work in step with your holiday operation, and every visit is documented for whoever asks — auditor, brand or corporate.
point_1_body: Moisture and food residue are a fly's ideal start.
point_2_body: Extra food and traffic mean extra risk.
point_3_body: Holiday overstock crowds out sanitation access.
note_body: Keep dry-storage spills cleaned and stock rotated through the busy weeks — stored-product pests establish fastest when sanitation slips under pressure.

subject: January is when the nest you missed becomes a colony
preheader: Peak rodent pressure meets targeted baiting and exclusion.
hero_alt: Rodent-burrow inspection along the building exterior
headline: JANUARY IS WHEN THE NEST YOU MISSED BECOMES A COLONY.
body_paragraph_1: January is when a nest you never saw in the fall turns into an established colony. Cold outside concentrates rodents indoors, and the quiet winter weeks give them time, warmth and cover.
body_paragraph_2: We treat the harborage and prove it's working — targeted baiting and exclusion where rodents live, plus monitors that show the population falling between visits, all on the record.
point_1_body: Ground burrows near the foundation are winter staging.
point_2_body: Warmth draws rodents to nest near equipment.
point_3_body: Wall bases and pipe chases are the travel routes.
note_body: Winter is the best time to find and seal exterior rodent entry, because activity concentrates the routes into a few obvious paths.

subject: Cold outside means crowded inside — for rodents
preheader: We treat the harborage and prove the population is dropping.
hero_alt: Interior bait/monitor check in a mechanical room
headline: COLD OUTSIDE MEANS CROWDED INSIDE — FOR RODENTS.
body_paragraph_1: Peak rodent pressure isn't dramatic — it's a population that got comfortable while the building focused on winter. The activity you'd have caught in October is now a routine behind the walls.
body_paragraph_2: We don't just set traps; we close the routes, remove the harborage and document the trend, so a peak-season problem is contained instead of managed forever.
point_1_body: Roof rats travel utility lines and overhangs.
point_2_body: Voids above tiles are prime winter nesting.
point_3_body: Break rooms feed the population overnight.
note_body: If monitor catches are rising month over month, the population is growing, not passing through — that's the signal to escalate, not wait.

subject: The quiet months are when infestations settle in
preheader: Monitors that tell us it's working between visits.
hero_alt: Tech documenting findings on a tablet in a stockroom
headline: THE QUIET MONTHS ARE WHEN INFESTATIONS GET ESTABLISHED.
body_paragraph_1: The infestations that cost the most got established in plain sight during the slow months. By deep winter, rodents have mapped your building better than most of your staff.
body_paragraph_2: One program, one invoice, and reporting that tells you the pressure is dropping — not just that someone showed up.
point_1_body: Mulch and shrubs against the wall hide the runs.
point_2_body: Quiet storage gives a colony room to grow.
point_3_body: Existing devices tell us if pressure is rising.
note_body: Clear clutter in mechanical rooms and stockrooms; a colony needs cover, and an organized room is a hostile one.

subject: Birds are scouting your roofline right now
preheader: Bird exclusion and early-season prep before nesting locks in.
hero_alt: Bird exclusion netting/spikes on a roofline ledge
headline: BIRDS ARE SCOUTING YOUR ROOFLINE RIGHT NOW.
body_paragraph_1: Before the first warm week, birds are already scouting your roofline, ledges and signage for nesting sites — and once eggs are present, exclusion becomes a protected, regulated headache instead of a simple fix.
body_paragraph_2: We handle bird exclusion — netting, spikes and deterrents — and get ahead of early invaders before nesting makes it complicated, with the documentation your file needs.
point_1_body: Flat ledges and signs are prime nesting perches.
point_2_body: Open eaves are a favorite protected nest site.
point_3_body: Occasional invaders emerge from perimeter gaps.
note_body: Get bird exclusion in place before eggs appear. Once a nest is active, the work becomes regulated, slower and more expensive.

subject: Exclusion is cheap before nesting season
preheader: We get ahead of the invaders before the first warm week.
hero_alt: Tech surveying rafters and ledges for nesting
headline: EXCLUSION IS CHEAP BEFORE NESTING. AFTER, IT'S PROTECTED.
body_paragraph_1: Late winter is the window between dormant and active. Occasional invaders are stirring in the voids and birds are prospecting outside, which makes now the cheapest, cleanest time to get ahead of both.
body_paragraph_2: We survey the roofline and voids, seal and exclude before activity peaks, and treat harborage at the source, so spring starts contained instead of chaotic.
point_1_body: HVAC units offer shelter and warmth for nests.
point_2_body: Covered docks invite roosting year-round.
point_3_body: Door sweeps and thresholds are early ant routes.
note_body: Late winter is the cheapest time to seal foundation and threshold gaps, before occasional invaders start moving out of the voids.

subject: The occasional invaders are waking up early
preheader: Roofline, ledges and entry points, surveyed and sealed.
hero_alt: Exterior eave and sign inspection with binoculars
headline: THE OCCASIONAL INVADERS ARE WAKING UP EARLY THIS YEAR.
body_paragraph_1: The pests of early spring announce themselves suddenly, but the groundwork is laid weeks earlier — on your roof, in your voids and around your foundation, while it still looks like winter.
body_paragraph_2: Exclusion and early prep run on one scope with a written record, so you're solving the problem now instead of protecting nests later.
point_1_body: Roof edges collect the debris birds build on.
point_2_body: Unscreened openings become nest entrances.
point_3_body: Overwintered pests move out through the same gaps.
note_body: Survey the roofline now for old nests and droppings; last year's sites are this year's, unless you exclude them first.

subject: The first warm week is the starting gun for ants
preheader: Exclusion and perimeter treatment before the spring surge.
hero_alt: Tech treating an exterior perimeter for ants
headline: THE FIRST WARM WEEK IS THE STARTING GUN FOR ANTS.
body_paragraph_1: Spring pests rarely 'arrive.' Ants, flies and occasional invaders emerge — from the voids, cracks and harborage they've occupied all winter — and the first warm week is the starting gun for the whole season.
body_paragraph_2: We treat the perimeter and the harborage and seal the entry points, so ants and flies are stopped at the source before they spread — with a record of every placement.
point_1_body: Ant trails start at foundation cracks and thresholds.
point_2_body: Leaks and damp areas draw ants and flies first.
point_3_body: Emerging flies collect at light and openings.
note_body: Seal thresholds and foundation cracks before the first warm week; the entry point you close in March is the ant trail you never chase in July.

subject: Spring pests don't arrive — they emerge from inside
preheader: We stop ants and flies at the source, not the surface.
hero_alt: Sealing a foundation crack / entry point
headline: SPRING PESTS DON'T ARRIVE. THEY EMERGE — FROM INSIDE.
body_paragraph_1: The first sustained warmth wakes everything at once. Ant colonies send out foragers, overwintered flies become active, and the entry points you didn't seal in fall become highways in March.
body_paragraph_2: We find the colonies' routes and the flies' breeding sites, exclude the entry points, and monitor the result, turning a spring surge into a non-event.
point_1_body: Door gaps are the first spring highway inside.
point_2_body: Spring fly breeding starts in neglected drains.
point_3_body: Overwintered colonies push foragers indoors.
note_body: Service floor drains and trash areas as temperatures rise — that's where the season's first fly generation actually starts.

subject: Seal it in March or chase it all summer
preheader: One scope, one invoice, a program on paper.
hero_alt: Fly-light service in an entryway
headline: SEAL IT IN MARCH OR CHASE IT ALL SUMMER.
body_paragraph_1: What you do before the surge decides the summer. Exclusion and perimeter work in March stops the problem at the source; wait, and you're chasing it across the building for months.
body_paragraph_2: One scope, one invoice, a program on paper — exclusion, perimeter and monitoring that get ahead of the season instead of chasing it.
point_1_body: Warmth pulls foragers through every seam.
point_2_body: Warming waste areas restart the fly cycle.
point_3_body: Beds against the wall are the launch point.
note_body: A single sustained warm spell can trigger emergence building-wide; getting exclusion done before it is the whole advantage.
